agent_notes: כָּסּוּ is Pual (morph HVPp3cp, gemination in the samekh): 'were covered', with הָרִים as subject and צִלָּהּ as accusative of the covering material, so 'mountains were covered [with] its shade'. This is Ibn Ezra's second option (cf. 'covers the naked with a garment'); his first option and Radak's 'like בצילה' supply a missing bet. Both give the same sense, but the grammar here needs no emendation. אַרְזֵי־אֵל is read as 'mighty/lofty cedars' (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion) with a divine-name element; the Hebrew has no 'like', so the simile in KJV/ASV is an insertion, and I bracket it only where English needs it.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses qetsir as 'branch'; the word usually means 'harvest'. I glossed it 'shoots/branches' following the parallel with yonqot and the commentators (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion citing Job 14:9).

The ayin of מִיָּעַר is written suspended in the Masoretic tradition (Rashi and Radak both remark on it, Meiri gives the midrashic play yeor/yaar). I translated the consonantal text as 'forest' and kept the tradition in the commentary and a note; the midrash itself is quoted only as the packet gives it.

זִיז is rare (here and Ps 50:11); I glossed it 'moving things' after Rashi's derivation from זָז and chose 'creatures that stir' in the literal layer. The five English versions all say 'wild beast(s)', which is a guess at the class, not a rendering of the root.

agent_notes: נָסוֹג is vocalized as an imperfect 'we will turn back' but Ibn Ezra raises the alternative that it is a past or a jussive-like form; I followed the plain imperfect with a negative, which all five English versions share.
The packet shows the Ketiv-less Masoretic pointing יְהוָה; I rendered the divine name as YHWH in the literal layer and the LORD in the dramatic layer, per the skill.

ולכה is read two ways. The masoretic note (reported by Rashi, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion, and by Ibn Ezra who rejects it) takes it as 'yours', i.e. לך, 'it falls to you'. Radak and Meiri read the plain verb 'go before us to save us'; Meiri records the 'yours' reading as a second option. The literal layer keeps the verb ('and come'), the commentary lays out both. STEPBible agrees with the verb (H1980).

The commentary names the Targum's paraphrase only through the packet text; I did not cite it for a claim. The Rashi on Ephraim/Manasseh/Benjamin (Aram, Joash, Esther) is mentioned only as the tradition's way of reading the three tribes; the plain sense (the tribes' order in the wilderness camp, Num 2) is my own reading and left without a source.
